name: Amira Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a milk tanker for the dairy co-op, collecting from farms up in the hills and bringing it back to the creamery in the valley. I start at five, do about nine farm collections, and at each one I test the milk, take a sample, hook up the hose and pump it into the tank. The lanes are narrow and the yards are muddy, so most of the skill is reversing a 26-tonne rigid truck past a gatepost with two centimetres to spare. I'm the senior driver on the hill round, so I also train the new ones on the sampling.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Jonah, my partner, who's in his last year as an apprentice electrician. We rent a cottage near the creamery and we've got about four months of savings. I use AI now and then, mostly when the co-op's forms make no sense and I want them in plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, and that the farmers would be glad too, because they're tired of being sold gadgets. In the drivers' group chat I'd say good, now can we talk about the shift patterns instead. Online I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep the job I'm good at, which is a big thing at twenty-seven. My bigger worry in that world is the co-op itself, because milk prices are rough and two small farms on my round sold up this year. Fewer farms means fewer collections, and that's my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the round and keep putting a hundred and fifty a month away. I'd go to the union branch meeting about the shift patterns, because the early starts are getting earlier. I might use one of the AI tools to help write the union's letter, since I do that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit wary about the farms. It's the normal kind of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which farms sold up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Pritchards at the top of the round, and a smaller one with forty cows. Old Mr Pritchard cried in the yard on my last pickup. When a dairy farm on my round sells up, I lose twenty minutes of work and the farmer loses three generations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would fewer farms change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. The co-op merges rounds when farms close, so the senior drivers keep their hours. If it got to three or four more, I'd start to worry.

say: I'd call it a **relief** and say the farmers are tired of gadgets.
I'd tell the group chat to focus on **shift patterns** instead.
think: I keep the **job I'm good at**, which matters at twenty-seven.
The real risk is **farms closing** on my round, which cuts my hours.
do: Keep the **hill round** and save a hundred and fifty a month.
Go to the **union branch** meeting about earlier start times.
Use an AI tool now and then to **draft letters**.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a familiar unease about the farms.
**Sad** about farmers selling up on her round.
S0.quote: When a dairy farm on my round sells up, I lose twenty minutes of work and the farmer loses three generations.
fieldNote: Her worry here is the **dairy economy**, not AI at all.
She uses AI **pragmatically** for paperwork without enthusiasm.
The Pritchard story shows she feels **close to the farmers** she serves.

steps.text: Keep driving the hill collection round for the co-op
Raise the early start times at the next union branch meeting
Save a hundred and fifty a month into the joint account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op office will change a lot and the drivers less, at least at first. I'd tell the newer drivers to learn the tablet properly when it comes, because the scheduling will all be on it. I'd also say we need the union in the room when they set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the sampling and the paperwork would go to software first. Right now I write down the temperature and volume, and the lab gets my sample; a smart tank could do all that itself. The driving and the hose work on muddy yards I'm not worried about yet. But if a tanker can test its own milk, they might decide they need fewer senior drivers to train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new scheduling system once the others in the depot had tried it and it worked. I'd ask the union to make sure training on it is paid time. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more, two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Interested in some of it, a bit annoyed that the skilled part of my job might shrink to just driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the job would you miss most if it went to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sampling, weirdly. It's the part where you notice a farm's milk is off before the lab does, and you can ring the farmer. A smart tank can record the milk temperature, but it won't ring Gwen (a farmer on her round) to say her cooler's playing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn it once others had tried it. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the co-op's last new system crashed for three weeks and we did everything twice. I'm not against it. I just want somebody else to find the bugs first.

say: I'd say the **co-op office** changes most and drivers change less at first.
I'd want the **union in the room** when the new system is set up.
think: Software will take the **sampling and paperwork** before the driving.
Fewer skilled tasks could mean fewer **senior drivers** needed for training.
do: Learn the **scheduling system** once others have tested it.
Ask the union for **paid training time** on new systems.
Raise savings to **two hundred** a month.
feel: **Mixed**: curious about some changes, annoyed at losing skilled work.
Slight **wariness** after the last system crashed.
S1.quote: A smart tank can record the milk temperature, but it won't ring Gwen (a farmer on her round) to say her cooler's playing up.
fieldNote: She values the **judgement** in her job, not just the driving.
Her waiting is about **bad experience** with systems, not fear of tech.
She expects her **senior role** to thin before her job does.

steps.text: Learn the co-op scheduling tablet after the first drivers test it
Ask the union branch for paid training time on new systems
Raise monthly savings from one hundred fifty to two hundred

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs a plan for drivers and farm workers before 2031, not after. In the union I'd push for proper notice and retraining money. Online I'd probably share things, but I'd be more careful with words at work, because the co-op managers are decent people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd give myself until about 2031 on the actual round. The thinking stuff goes in 2028: scheduling, sampling records, route planning, maybe the farm payments too. Then robots in 2031, and a tanker that drives itself up the main valley road is easy. The narrow lanes and gateposts might buy a year or two more, but not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start the driving instructor qualification, because teaching people to drive feels like it lasts longer than driving itself. I'd keep the round while I train, and push savings up to six months. I'd also sit down with Jonah and check what we'd live on if I earned less for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I like having a plan, and the instructor idea feels like one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would people still need driving lessons if trucks drive themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cars and vans won't all change at once, and people will still want a licence for years. I'm not certain, but it's the best bet I can see from where I sit. If I'm wrong about driving lessons lasting, at least I'll have spent the robot years teaching nervous seventeen-year-olds instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Jonah? Does his work help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His trade feels safer than mine. Rewiring old houses is fiddly, and he says robots will struggle with what's behind a hundred-year-old wall. If I had to earn less for a year, his wage could carry the rent.

say: I'd call for a **government plan** for drivers and farm workers before 2031.
I'd push the union for **notice and retraining** money but stay polite at work.
think: I'd give the round until about **2031**, with paperwork gone in 2028.
The **narrow lanes** might buy a year or two, but not a career.
do: Start the **driving instructor** qualification in the first year.
Keep the round while training and push savings to **six months**.
Check with Jonah what they'd live on on **one wage**.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadied by having a plan.
**Unsure** whether the instructor bet will hold.
S2.quote: If I'm wrong about driving lessons lasting, at least I'll have spent the robot years teaching nervous seventeen-year-olds instead of waiting.
fieldNote: She thinks clearly about the **thinking-then-robots** gap and plans around it.
Her partner's trade gives the household a **second leg** to stand on.
She admits **uncertainty** about her instructor bet rather than overselling it.

steps.text: Enrol in the driving instructor qualification this year
Build savings to six months while still driving the round
Join the union push for notice periods and retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly, so let's not waste it. At the union I'd ask for a transition agreement with the co-op: retraining paid for, and notice before any self-driving tankers come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives me until about 2034 on the round, which is seven years. That's long enough to finish the instructor course without rushing and build up some pupils on the side. The thinking parts of the job, the scheduling and the records, would be software by 2031, and I'd just be the driver for the last few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the instructor qualification over two years, evenings and weekends, and start teaching on Saturdays. I'd keep saving, two hundred a month. I'd try the co-op's AI tools when they arrived, because knowing them might help me get a job overseeing the self-driving fleet if that's a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the two-year one. Still anxious about the end, but there's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather stay at the co-op or leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay, if they'd have me in some role. I know the farms and the farmers, and that's worth something even when the truck drives itself. Somebody has to fix things when the tanker gets stuck in a yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the new drivers you train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get another skill alongside, no shame in it. I'd tell the new tanker drivers I train to get a second skill now, because I'm learning one at twenty-seven and wish I'd started at twenty.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to do this properly.
I'd ask for a **transition agreement** with the co-op on retraining and notice.
think: I'd have until about **2034** on the round, seven years from now.
By 2031 I'd be **just the driver**, with scheduling and records automated.
do: Train as a **driving instructor** over two years of evenings.
Start **teaching on Saturdays** for extra income.
Try the co-op's **AI tools** to aim for a fleet oversight role.
S3.quote: I'd tell the new tanker drivers I train to get a second skill now, because I'm learning one at twenty-seven and wish I'd started at twenty.
fieldNote: She'd use the time for a **side income** that could become the main one.
Loyalty to the **co-op and farmers** keeps her hoping to stay.
Her advice to new drivers reveals some **regret** about starting late.

steps.text: Complete the driving instructor course over two years of evenings
Teach driving lessons on Saturdays once qualified
Try each new co-op AI tool in its first month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Ten years is time for real retraining schemes, and I'd want the union and the government to set them up early. I'd say that at work and anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels long. Robots in 2039 makes me thirty-nine or forty, and I could have a whole instructing business by then, or move into something else completely. The office side of the co-op changes in 2036, and I'd probably still be on the round then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the round for now and save. In a couple of years I'd do the instructor course, no rush. I'd pick up the AI tools as they become normal. Jonah and I would probably buy a place in this one, since we'd have more certainty for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Uneasy at the back of my mind, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start the instructor course sooner if you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, to be honest. I'd tell myself there's loads of time, and then it's 2033 and I'm scrambling. Jonah would nag me, which is useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would buying a place mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the thing we keep putting off because we don't know what's coming. With ten years of warning, Jonah (her partner) and I could finally stop renting and buy somewhere near the creamery.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **nobody an excuse** for skipping retraining.
I'd want **early schemes** from the union and government.
think: By **2039** I could have an instructing business or a new career.
The **office changes** in 2036 would barely affect my round.
do: Keep the round and **save** for now.
Take the **instructor course** in a couple of years.
**Buy a house** near the creamery with Jonah.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a quiet worry at the back of her mind.
Wary of her own **complacency** with so much time.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, Jonah (her partner) and I could finally stop renting and buy somewhere near the creamery.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her make **family plans** like buying a home.
She expects to **delay** retraining and relies on her partner to push her.
Her job feels **safe for now** but clearly not for good.

steps.text: Buy a house near the creamery with Jonah within three years
Take the driving instructor course around 2029
Keep the hill round and save two hundred a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years for the paperwork and five for the driving isn't long enough to switch to teaching and build pupils. What would help is the co-op paying for retraining while I still drive, so I'm not choosing between wage and course. Pay me to learn my next job while I still do this one, and I'll leave the tanker without a fight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the farms. Self-driving tankers won't happen in a vacuum; if the farms on my round close, the co-op won't need robots or drivers. The milk price matters as much as any AI.

headlineQuote: Pay me to learn my next job while I still do this one, and I'll leave the tanker without a fight.
portrait: A **27-year-old** senior milk tanker driver collecting from hill farms for a dairy co-op.
She rents with her **apprentice electrician** partner Jonah and has four months saved.
In a quiet world she worries about **farms closing**, not AI.
In the AGI pictures she plans to become a **driving instructor** while still driving.
Ten years would let her **buy a home**, though she admits she'd delay retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there isn't time to retrain and build pupils before driving goes.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op **paying for retraining** while she still drives the round.
Attention to **milk prices**, since farm closures cut her work too.
